title: Count the Equal Pairs

concept.title: Count the earlier partners
body: A pair of positions `i < j` with `a[i] == a[j]` is "good". Instead of testing every pair, look at each number `x` when you reach it: it forms one good pair with **every earlier copy of `x`**. A map `seen` stores how many copies of each value came before.
The answer can be large: if all 20000 numbers are equal, there are about 2 * 10^8 pairs, so use 64-bit integers in C++ and Java.

statement: Count the pairs of positions `i < j` in an array of `n` integers with `a[i] = a[j]`.
hints: Trying all pairs takes about n * n / 2 steps.
When you read a number, the pairs it completes are the earlier copies of it.
Keep a map with the number of copies seen so far, and add that number to the answer.

explanation: Each number forms a pair with every earlier equal number. A map of counts gives that number in O(1), so one pass is enough.
solution.complexity: Time O(n) on average, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

seen = {}
total = 0
for x in a:
    total += seen.get(x, 0)
    seen[x] = seen.get(x, 0) + 1
print(total)
